utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom, in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I am informed that the Defence wanted to address the Chamber. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Mr. President, I am just being reminded, Ms. Pilipovic has asked me that if we can cross-examine the witness in tandem for practical and technical reasons, and I am thinking in advance for your decision. Now, the reason why we wanted to address your Chamber is the following: Very soon, we are to hear a witness -- excuse me. We are going to hear a witness here whose name -- who is Vahid Karavelic. And in relation to this witness, the Defence has just received - that is, received it yesterday - received a supplementary information sheet yesterday concerning this witness. First of all, as far as the form is concerned, I understand that the courtesy has gone right out of this courtroom, which I regret very much. I believe that this document was drafted by the Prosecution, and I can read some rather unpleasant things. I don't think that it is not forbidden that if we are to -- if we are talking about an accused who is presumed innocent, that we speak of an accused as a "Mr. Galic" or a "General Galic," but just to speak of him as "Galic," Mr. President and Your Honours, this rather shows a rather lack of courtesy. I think that this is a question of form and I think that we should re-invent courtesy here. That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...ask you, if there is something that you would not like to happen in this courtroom, until now, as far as I can see, we are not informed about anything in respect of the Witness Karavelic. If you could solve the matter with the Prosecutor, then whatever is unpleasant will not come to the eyes or to the ears of the Court. What you are doing now is to introduce something which comes from the Prosecution and which is not yet known to the Court. If you could prevent it from coming to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will do my best, Mr. President. Thank you. But the reason why we should intervene is the following: In this supplementary information that we received yesterday, we can see that there is a number of things that seem extraordinary, to say the least. This is a high officer, Lieutenant General, or a General, who was normally interviewed by the Prosecution a few months ago, and we can see that a few days before the end of the case, this witness who is certainly being worked by or supported by three parties present at the interview, is saying in a very determined way like there were never any mortars in Sarajevo, claiming that only some vehicles were used, saying that in relation to some manufacturing plants of weapons ammunition, that this is not true, and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, as you noticed, the Chamber just conferred. We are now confronted with some arguments on a witness we have not heard yet, and although I see that he is scheduled on the list, I do not know whether whatever is in your papers will be his testimony in this Court. The Chamber thinks that it is not proper to discuss evidence, or potential evidence, which has not been presented yet and which even might not be presented at all. So, therefore, if you could inform us about the purpose of your intervention and it could not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to discuss what is in any additional written statement of the potential witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will, Mr. President. The objective of my intervention is to say the following: There is a decision which took place in January of this year in case Naletilic, Tuta, IT-98-48-T, which rejected certain information that was tardily given by the Prosecution. We believe that we are in a very similar situation to that one, even comparable situation. And what we want to say is that bearing in mind this new information, this new piece of information which arrived very belatedly, and are trying to cover what the Defence has managed to show so far, that is, trying to show the opposite of what the Prosecution was saying. Now, if the witness is heard by your Chamber, and bearing in mind the rather extraordinary evidence that he is going to give after three representatives from the Prosecution interviewed him, we believe that it will be the duty of your Chamber to remind him -- express provisions about what will happen if he gives false testimony. I believe that it is 98 or 99 -- Rule 98 or 99 which is dealing with false testimony, and we will ask before this witness testifies that he is very clearly informed of the consequences of what we call false testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The Chamber will consider whether it is appropriate to do this prior to testimony given or during testimony in Court. And at least it takes another month, as far as I can see, before this witness is scheduled to testify in this Court. So we have some time to consider the matter. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have nothing to add, Mr. President. We are ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are ready to proceed. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Briquemont. Perhaps it is not necessary, but I would like to draw your attention to the fact that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. [In English] Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I have a number of documents to show to the witness. I wonder if that could most efficiently be done by giving them to the witness sequentially and individually, or perhaps in one large bundle and the witness going through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If no confusion is created, Mr. Ierace, I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will start off doing it one by one and see how we go with time. I ask the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 1740. While that's being done, perhaps I can ask the witness a question

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good morning, General. Could you tell us who Viktor Andreev was?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ierace. Viktor Andreev was a Civil Affairs who was the representative of the representative of the Secretary General of the United Nations, and as soon as he arrived, he told me that he had many difficulties to work in his hierarchy or chain of command, if I can call it the chain of command, and that he was placing himself completely at my disposal. He helped me as much as he could. He was Russian, so he could speak easily or more easily than others. He was able to speak with the Serbs. And I was taking into consideration all of these aspects of the way my collaborators work. But certainly, he always helped me working as a deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpreted] For the transcript, you said that Mr. Andreev, that he was the representative of the representative of the representative. That's just for the transcript

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I should not try to express myself this way but I was just trying to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpreted] That is very well, but the transcript says representative of the Secretary General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he was not the representative of the Secretary General, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Briquemont, you were asked who Mr. Andreev was, and you answered that question and you gave quite some additional information on the person. This Chamber is aware that the Prosecution is under some time restraint and might be interested in specific information you would not think of, and on the other hand, the Chamber might perhaps already have been aware of other information you are giving. Could I ask to listen carefully to the questions of the Prosecution, answer them, and if there is any additional information, whether he spoke the language or not, it might be that the Prosecution is highly interested to know, they will ask you. But perhaps they have totally different purpose of putting that question to you, for example, to know his age or to know when he arrived. So would you please listen carefully to the question and then answer to that specific question, and whatever other information is needed, the Prosecution certainly will ask you. This is not to be impolite to you, but we are under heavy time restraint and that is the reason why I am asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No need to excuse. But please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General, could you tell us who a gentleman by the name of De Mello was?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sergio De Mello was officially the representative of the representative of the Secretary General of the United Nations and he was a deputy of Mr. Stoltenberg.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this stage, it would be appropriate to go into closed session, given the nature of the document. There are one or two others of the same category and I will deal with all of those together. I imagine we will be in closed session for approximately 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we then turn into closed session. I see it is confirmed on my screen that we are in closed session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I ask the witness be shown Exhibit P1522.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General, in relation to this document, does it appear to be the first Igman agreement which was signed on the 11th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that the agreement, Mr. Ierace, is the military part of the peace agreement of Mr. Stoltenberg and Lord Owen. If I see the date -- if you look at the first page, it says: Designed to work out arrangements for bringing about compliance," and so forth, the cessation of hostilities and so on. So I believe that this was the agreement -- well, the military aspect of the peace agreement that Mr. Stoltenberg hoped to present to the three parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: My apology for that. You are quite correct. If you could please turn to page 7 of that document. We see the signatures of General Mladic and yourself amongst others on the agreement.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might that be returned. And might the witness be shown Exhibit 2082.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, is this a letter from you addressed to Dr. Karadzic dated the 8th of January, 1994, in which you inform him that a crater analysis of a shell impact on Sarajevo airport which occurred on the 5th of January, you believed to demonstrate conclusively that the source of the fire was from the side occupied by the Serb military, in particular, it emanated from the area of Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I don't have to make any comment in relation to this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might that be returned. Might the witness be shown Exhibit P1928.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, may I just ask you, the document just shown to the witness, P2082, contains two letters and annexes. Are they -- do they have any relevance because you didn't ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No. And I am mindful of the time, Mr. President. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So this first letter, the front page --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will be seeking to tender the bundle. I think that those documents speak for themselves in relation to the same incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then of course just to -- I mean, the second page, I take it that you want to then verify that this is a letter that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. came from --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I am happy to do that, Mr. President, if you think it appropriate. Might that document be returned to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please turn to the following page? And do we see a letter, also addressed from you, on this occasion to President Izetbegovic on the same date, complaining of attacks or the use of artillery in and around the airport and a warning which you delivered to him that the humanitarian airlift will be suspended unless you receive his assurances that such an attack would not be repeated?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter is correct. My worry, Mr. Ierace, was that every time a shell exploded not very far from the airport, the people from NATO said that they wouldn't come again to bring humanitarian aid. So I was doing my best with both sides in order to avoid all shelling in the vicinity of the airport because the humanitarian aid was meant for the whole city of Sarajevo, in fact, for the whole of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may the witness be shown P1955.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. But if we look at these two letters, we see that they do not have an annex, and now that you mention it, the entire bundle of the documents that is presented by the Prosecution, there are three other documents that were not officially annexed to either of the letters. So I don't know what Mr. Ierace proposes to do with this bundle and these documents, whether he is going to tender them or not tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, to the other documents as well, and I see a map where it identified that there is at least part of Sarajevo on it but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in order to save time, I don't -- I won't tender this document in due course. I think the relevant parts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The relevant parts. Okay. Then you will indicate what these are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to correct that, what I propose to do is not take those documents any further with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The relevant parts or, rather, the parts upon which I rely have now gone into evidence through the oral evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the witness have 1955? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General, in front of you do you have --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, Mr. Ierace, I have before me two documents, P1928 and the P1955. So I have two documents before me.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I will deal with 1928 first. Is 1928 a letter from General Delic, addressed to you, complaining -- dated the 6th of December 1993, complaining that the city, that is the city of Sarajevo, had received heavy shelling? And I refer you to the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, this letter is dated the 6th of December, so the day that General Delic sent me this letter, his troops launched three attacks in Sarajevo against held positions. I have to say that the development of the head of the Muslim army was very clear in this month of December. He was convinced that the Muslim forces were sufficiently well-organised in order to be able to resume their offensive anywhere, either in Central Bosnia or in Sarajevo. I have to say receiving this letter on the 6th of December in the evening was very strange for me. In fact, General Delic authorised himself to launch attacks from Sarajevo and he was asking me to intervene with the Serbs in order not to respond. This was the kind of letter to which I didn't really attach much importance. I saw General Delic again immediately in order to discuss this problem. It has to be made very clear, I believe, for the Tribunal, that in December both sides were determined to continue the war because there was no peace agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General, if I could perhaps clarify the interest of the Tribunal to you. In terms of blame or fault - with your leave, Mr. President - the primary interest is, one might say, is in whether or not there were attacks either deliberately or indiscriminately on civilian targets or civilian areas. In your answer, you referred to the steps taken by General Delic to continue to prosecute the armed conflict. But my question is directed to simply, in the first instance, whether that is what General Delic said in his letter, that is, he complained that the city had been exposed to heavy shelling. I think your -- perhaps if you could just focus on that question and agree or disagree that that is what the letter expresses.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I am trying to answer your question as clearly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, would it be appropriate at this stage to direct the witness to answer the question? I am very conscious of the time limits that the Prosecution is working under.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness indicated that he was trying to answer the question as clearly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the General was about to say that he wanted to answer the question. And let us let him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...decide on the suggestion of Mr. Ierace. Could you please answer the question, that is, whether this letter indicates that General Delic was sending you a letter in which he says that Sarajevo has been exposed to heavy shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is certain that the city of Sarajevo on the 6th of December was shelled, but the troops, Muslim troops, launched at 4, 6, and 8 in the morning, attacks from the city. The Serbs responded. How do you want to avoid shelling of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General, could I direct your attention to some specific words in the letter, and again I emphasise I am simply asking at this stage whether the letter states certain things. In the first paragraph, does General Delic refer to "all available weapons having been used during the past days," that is days plural, "including combat aircraft," and then in brackets does he say: "Yesterday we talked about it." End brackets. "The city of Sarajevo has been exposed to heavy shelling." In other words, I am not asking you at this stage whether General Delic was at fault, but simply whether they were the terms of his complaint to you in this letter dated the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say in the first paragraph and when you read the words "including combat aircraft," combat aircraft was never used in Bosnia among the parties, at least during my period of command, by either parties. So in this first paragraph, we can see that it is a paragraph which is over-dramatising the situation. But I do repeat, Sarajevo was shelled in a much more intense way in the month of December. So this part of the letter does correspond to the reality, but what General Delic doesn't say is that he himself launched the offences from the city of Sarajevo against the Serbs

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...Mr. Ierace. When you read the words "where all available weapons have been used," what would that refer to? I mean, in your question, it is not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President. There are other cities referred to as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would "where" not refer to the other cities?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. It is not clear where the combat aircraft was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then please --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is there, when I read it, it is: Beside the offensive activities of the Serb aggressor in the area of responsibility of the cities of Tuzla, Zivinice, Kalesija and Teocak, where all available weapons have been used." So beside the offensives there, where all weapons have been used, "The city of Sarajevo has been exposed to heavy shelling." Or am I wrong in reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General, in general terms, in relation to that first week in December, you have told us so far that there was shelling of the city of Sarajevo, that at some stage, either before, during or after that shelling, there was an offensive by the government forces, and that offensive was conducted with the objective of cutting the Pale road. Is that the case? I withdraw that. Is it your evidence, as I understand it, that there was shelling of the city of Sarajevo that week and at some stage there was an offensive by the government military forces that week as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, during --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking about -- I am sorry, Mr. Ierace. When you are talking about the government, you mean the Bosnian government of Sarajevo. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now during that shelling of Sarajevo by the Serb military forces, firstly, regardless of which part of those forces did it, were civilian targets hit in the city?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene, but the French booth is correcting itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question, Mr. Briquemont? It is where --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no doubt that during the shelling the civilians were hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now my next question is: Did it appear to you that those civilian targets hit by the shelling coming from the Serb side were deliberately hit?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that when two sides were responding, one to the actions of the other, they were in fact targeting military targets. I am trying to think of some areas, particularly in order to retake some areas, particularly those that were dominating the city. Here I have to give you an explanation which would be of a military aspect. I was really struck by the age of the ammunition that was used for Sarajevo. Some of the shells never exploded --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If I can interrupt you there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like the General to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As you please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Briquemont.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think perhaps this is a technical matter. But when one fires very old ammunition, there is a lot that can happen. It can misfire, it wouldn't work. So I can give you some explanation that we believed at the Main Staff, we thought that 10 to 20 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. per cent of the shells never exploded. On the other hand, when you have a bad functioning of the weapons, then some of these shells wouldn't fall exactly where they were meant to fall. So when we want to make a very honest assessment of what happened in Sarajevo, one has to bear in mind about some technical aspects. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General, I appreciate you explaining in general terms of what happened in terms of the quality of the artillery shells, but my question is in relation to that week, to the civilian targets being hit, and simply whether or not you had a view, you had an opinion, as to whether the civilian targets had been deliberately hit? In other words, had they been targeted deliberately?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I already answered this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that completes examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Ms. Pilipovic, is it you who is going to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour, I will start examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, let me remind you that we had asked for authorisation to work in tandem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree. As you know, that has no consequences as far as the time is concerned. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, yesterday we started your testimony practical by you looking at the Resolution of the Security Council, 836, dated 4th of June, 1993. And yesterday, on page 59 of the transcript, line 69, you said that as a General, you never could understand the actual resolution. I am interpreting your words. Could you please confirm if this is what you said?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In the course of the examination-in-chief by my learned colleague, at one point you said that you would give a better interpretation of the resolution if you had a look at it, or rather if you had a copy with you.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to show -- point out the ambiguities in the resolution where they spoke both of legitimate defence, but legitimate defence is something we always have. But I especially wanted to point out what was realistic when the Security Council said that in a light version, and I think that I said to the Tribunal that as a General, "light version" didn't mean anything in operation -- didn't mean anything in operational terms. That I had been promised 6.000 men, that that was the only way to be able to receive reinforcements and the -- in personnel, and the only way to ensure the defence of the safe zones. And I can tell you that Defence means very much something different for us military people as the diplomats in New York. I repeat that it was an extremely ambiguous resolution which was very difficult for the Security Council to sign, and for the military personnel that it was and for General Cot, didn't really mean anything at all any more when we looked at how things were really happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: He said, "unrealistic," not "realistic."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, the Defence would ask you to have a look at the resolution dated 4th of June 1993, Resolution 836. The Defence has copied part of the resolution, page 3. I would like you -- if you can clarify the items 5 and 6 of the resolution.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask the usher, the page 3 of the resolution, that is the number of the exhibit of the Prosecution is P3715. For practical reasons, we copied items 5 and 6. Your Honour, considering that the Prosecution has made a proposal that as an exhibit the P3715 would be tendered as an exhibit, we just copied that page, the relevant page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, you have before you page 3 of 836 Resolution. First of all, I would like to ask you to read item 5 of the resolution.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me to read out loud, is that what you are asking?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If you find item 5 clear, then you can just interpret for us item 5 of the said Resolution.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I would like to read it very quickly, read the paragraph very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read the paragraph. These are words which from the point that I was not receiving any reinforcements in military terms no longer had any significance, at least when I was being asked to deter attacks against the safe areas, to promote the withdrawal and so on or the ceasefire monitors. For that, I would have needed thousands of additional men, men I didn't have. Have I answered your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, General. Thank you. General, could you tell us within item 5, considering that what is mentioned is defence resistance to attack of protected areas, you as a General and a military expert, can you clarify or at least explain what is meant by the term "protected area"?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The safe areas that were determined, as I said yesterday, for five cities, Sarajevo, Tuzla, Gorazde, Zepa and Srebrenica, these were the areas where we were supposed to protect the population, preventing any attacks on those zones or areas. I think there was two areas where we succeeded in determining the exact limits of the safe areas, that is Srebrenica and -- but there were even challenges about that in the south of that and around Zepa. When I arrived in Sarajevo, and I said that yesterday, General Morillon was making an effort in order to exactly delineate on the ground what the borders of the safe areas were as regards Sarajevo. It was essential for us military people to determine those lines. When the politicians or the diplomats had used a pencil in order to mark out the thickness of what was written, the pencil already represented several kilometres. And so were never able to delineate exactly on the ground what the limits of the safe areas were and this caused constant and eternal discussions and in fact, I would say that I interpreted somewhat as the commander in chief what the limits were, and those limits in the end did -- corresponded to the areas occupied by the parties, both the parties, facing one another, but did not certainly correspond to any limit, any border, which would allow us to carry out the mission which had been given to us by the Security Council. To do so, we would have had to have withdrawals or advances by one or other of the other parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see you are looking --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a good moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, before the break, we spoke about the safe areas and you told us that Sarajevo, on the basis of Resolution 836, also was a safe area. General, can you tell us if Sarajevo, as a city, could be considered a protected safe area?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo was the city, the safe area, which I was really -- if I had to best protect it because that is where I had the most troops. Asserting that it was protected with the troops that I had, I would say no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, when you speak of the city of Sarajevo, do you -- did you understand by the term of "protected zone of Sarajevo," understand the area under the control of the BiH army or also the part of the city which was under the control of the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear that in my mind the safe area of Sarajevo was to be or should have included the crests which overlook -- or the ridges that overlook Sarajevo but I have already explained that it was never possible to define exactly what the limits of the safe area, of the regular or normal safe area, of Sarajevo were. And on the ground, in fact, the safe area was, in fact, the one that was occupied by the Muslim -- the Bosnian Muslim troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, when you came to the city of Sarajevo, were you aware that the city of Sarajevo was composed of 10 municipalities?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was familiar with the general organisation of Sarajevo, but when you say "municipalities," if I could compare with that a city like Paris, they were more "arrondisements" with local mayors, but I knew that the city of Sarajevo was composed of a whole group of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you knew that the city of Sarajevo had a whole series of municipalities, as far as you remember and on the basis of the information you received during your stay in Sarajevo, were you aware of how the city of Sarajevo was divided? To be more precise, did you know which parts of the city of Sarajevo were under the control of the Serb army and which parts under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we had a relatively exact idea of the areas occupied respectively by the Serbs, Muslims and even the Croats. Because the Croats who were fighting with the Muslims and that more or less coincided with the contact line or the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, you told us today that the safe area which you controlled was the area under the control of the Muslim army. Can you confirm to us that the Muslim soldiers used the protection of the UN to organise their soldiers in those safe areas?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have already answered that question. It is clear that as of October or November of 1993, and I pointed this out in reports to the highest United Nations authorities, in which I told them that the safe areas were becoming a trap for the UN troops because if the Muslim troops took advantage of those areas in order to organise themselves and to launch operations, military operations, from the safe areas, we were completely out of -- we were completely skewed in respect of Security Resolution 836. The documents are well-known, and I could even refer to what I say in my book, where I almost completely repeated a document that was sent in January to the United Nations authorities in order to point out the dangers of that trap.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, as far as I have understood you, the Muslims abused the protection of the UN in the safe areas to organise their own army and to launch attacks from those safe areas. Can you explain to us what were the UN and UNPROFOR motives to allow such illegal activities of the Muslim army in the safe areas?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I leave you the responsibility for the word "abuse." And that is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the whole problem of this Resolution 836. I never had the military assets which were sufficient in order to prevent either of the parties from militarily organising itself. And if I can illustrate the problem to the Tribunal, I would say that my mandate, at the very best of things or the very worst of things, was limited to humanitarian assistance. And that by going to Mount Igman, I was already beyond the mandate that had been given to me. It was never modified. And so I would say that I never had the assets which would allow me to prevent either of the warring parties from organising itself, from provoking things or from launching military operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, are you telling us that according to you, UNPROFOR did not fulfill its mandate in respect of Sarajevo as a protected area in accordance with Resolution 836?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I said one day in Sarajevo during a radio broadcast that I didn't even continue to read the Security Council resolutions because they were of absolutely no use to me. Now, you can conclude from that that the UNPROFOR troops were not in a position to carry out their mission. I would simply add that in order to carry out a mission, one must have the means in order to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. General, can you confirm to us that on July 12th, when you came to Sarajevo in 1993, whether you were informed that operations Lukavac 93 was being conducted by the Bosnian Serb army and that operation included Jahorina, Treskavica, Bjelasnica, Trnovo, and started from July to August, 1993, and all three warring factions took part in that operation?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived on the 12th of July, I was briefed about the situation. I believe that there was a war which was widespread all over Bosnia, but it was in central Bosnia between the Croats and Muslims and all around Sarajevo. I don't remember a specific briefing in respect of the cities that you have just mentioned. All I know is that at the end of July, the Serb troops launched a very significant operation in order to surround Sarajevo by taking control over Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, were you informed, when coming to Sarajevo, about what kind of army and what was the number of soldiers under the control of the BH army in the Igman area?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I would first say that the United Nations did not allow us to have an intelligence service. Of course, that was an order we did not respect. We tried as much as possible to have one. When I arrived in Sarajevo, General Morillon transmitted to me a description as accurately as possible of what the situation was. I was -- I knew him very well. We had gone to the war college together in Paris. And so he gave me as much information as he had. And when we spoke about the troops fighting on the ground, it was an estimate, more or less correct, because once again, in order to know the number of units fighting on the ground, one has to have an effective intelligence service, which is something which we of course did not have in the beginning of July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, you are telling us that you were informed and given an assessment by Mr. Morillon about the persons who took part in the operations. Can you tell us whether you received information about how many soldiers the 1st Corps of the BiH army had which covered a part of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did have information at the time but rather than giving an imaginary figure, I would prefer saying to you that I don't remember any more exactly what that number was. I will give you an explanation now which might be more complete. When one speak about a battalion and armies, that means about 800 men. And after some time, we realise that a battalion, whether it for the Serb or Croat or Muslim battalion, that represented only sometimes 150 men. They also spoke about army corps. But for us that meant 20.000 or 25.000 men. But on the ground, maybe there was 3.000 or 4.000 or 5.000. I am also saying that the Muslim army was being reorganised further to General Delic's orders, so I would say that specific figures are not something that I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, if I tell you that the 1st Corps of the BiH army in the documents that the Defence has as a UN report in Sarajevo, that there were there brigades of the 1st Corps of the BiH army, that there was a special -- that there were special forces and that there was also an artillery unit, the number of persons ranged from 25.000 and 45.000. Did you have such information and can you confirm whether such an information was correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were several brigades. You could also mention the Croat brigade. If in the United Nations' reports they speak -- they mention those numbers, well, you know, going through 20 to 25 -- figures, I would say 20.000 to 45.000 don't mean very much. I don't know how now these figures are particularly significant for me as a United Nations chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, were you informed about the zone of responsibility of the 1st Corps? I apologise, when I say, "1st Corps," I mean the 1st Corps of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had understood your question. But I suppose that the zone of responsibility of the 1st Corps had been set by General Delic, who was not really obliged to inform me of which limits he had set for his 1st Corps. But I suppose that his zone of responsibility was to defend the Sarajevo zone which he controlled. I don't really know what other zone of responsibility he might have had.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, when I asked you the question about the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps, I thought that you had been informed of the different strategic locations who were under the control of the 1st Corps of the BiH army and which affected the course of fighting which took part in the part of the city of Sarajevo. If I tell you that the main strategic points in the part of Sarajevo which was under the control of the 1st Corps of the BH army was Hum, Zuc, Kordun [phoen], Mojmilo, Golo Brdo, Prijedor [phoen] Brdo, Igman, Colina Kapa, mala and big, and Dolac Brdo, would you say that this information given to you by the Defence about the strategic points under the control of the BH army was a correct piece of information?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. These are names that remind me of something. One might even add Stup, which was south-west of Zuc. So I think that what you are saying is more or less correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your view, what was the strategic and operational importance of the party, of the side, that held these under its control?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit I don't really quite understand that question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you rephrase it, Ms. Pilipovic, so that the witness understands.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, we agreed that the important areas were Dolac, Preda [phoen], Hum, Mojmilo, Golo Brdo, Colina Kapa and Velika Mala, were areas which were under the control of the 1st Corps of the BH army. If I tell you that these areas were areas from which a part of the city of -- that was an area of the city very much under the control of the BH army, could you tell us that an army that controls such important strategic areas is -- had control of that area?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will answer from a military point of view. For me, the most important part among those parts was Mount Igman because Mount Igman had the most important ridges, from which one controlled or could completely control the city. And I would say that for the Bosnian army, that is the Muslims, the Mount Igman had an essential significance because Mount Igman controlled the only road allowing the Sarajevo Muslims to have contact with the outside world through the tunnel that went under the airport and then the roads, or one or two roads, which crossed the wooded area of Mount Igman toward Tarcin, et cetera. And that is why the agreement on Mount Igman was so important for the Bosnian army, and General Delic realised this very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, when we speak about the brigades of the 1st Corps of the BiH army, can you tell us on the basis of your recollection how much were you informed about the command points of the 1st Corps of the BiH army and the headquarters of -- how well were you informed about the deployment of the command post of that army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that the only person I spoke with was General Delic. In Sarajevo was the Sector Sarajevo commander who dealt with both the parties, that is either the Serbs or Muslims, from the point of view of the details of the headquarters. The only one of those headquarters which was very important for me was the 1st Bosnian Corps headquarters, which was on Mount Igman at the time that we signed the agreement. The others, or the location of the other headquarters, was not so important for me because headquarters in operations move around, depending on the fighting. And the exact location of those headquarters did not concern me very much as a commander in chief of the United Nations troops in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, could you tell us, for the United Nations observers who were in Sarajevo positioned on the side, on the Papa side, on the side of the Bosnian Serb army, that is for the United Nations monitors who were on that side, how important for the proper reporting, how important was it to know the command posts, not only of the brigades but also of the battalions and companies of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter correction: Not the Bosnian Serb side, but the BH side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The most important for the United Nations observers was to know the contact line between the Serbs and the Muslims, and we knew -- but perhaps we should look at the Sarajevo Sector maps again. We knew the United Nations units that were in Sarajevo. They knew more or less what the limits between the brigades were, that is the Bosnian brigades, because we had quite a few problems with the presence of the Croat brigade in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, when you say that the observers had to know the demarcation lines of the warring sides, could you tell us, according to you, from a military aspect, on one side, how deep goes the brigade area?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. I don't have a map any more that I can use. By memory, I could not tell you what the limits of the units were in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, in principal, could you tell us the depth of the front of one brigade?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I am going to tell you what I have already said. Without a situation map, I am not able to answer precisely for this Tribunal. Mr. President, it goes back nine years and I cannot answer this type of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It needs no explanation. If you don't know, just tell us and -- or if you do not remember. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Now, General, if I tell you that in the course of the proceedings Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. before this Chamber in this case we heard many United Nations observers and we were not able to get from them data and information on the positions of the brigades of the 1st Corps, of the command posts of the battalions of the companies of the 1st Corps of the BH army, nor of the brigades, could you confirm that their reporting, in respect of the shelling that they were saying was coming from the Serb side, could not be precise when we are talking about the shelling of facilities in the city, of the part of the city which was under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I object to that question, Mr. President. It is a non sequitur. The question works from the premise that because, as my learned colleague remembers it, UNMOs were not able to give information in these court proceedings as to the positions of the brigades of the 1st Corps or the command posts, then the proposition continues, the shelling information which they conveyed to the Tribunal or recorded at the time was imprecise. It is a question which simply doesn't make sense. In any event, I challenge the presumption -- the premise, rather. It is my recollection that there was evidence as to the position of the command posts and some of the brigades from some of the UN witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have had some difficulties, and perhaps some of the other members of the Chamber as well, of the logic of your introduction of the question and then the question itself, since the introduction was about position and knowledge of the brigades, while the question then later was about the source of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will rephrase my question. I will rephrase my question in a sense that I would like the General to tell us if it was acceptable for the observers of the United Nations, for their area of responsibility, they did not have precise data on the positions of the command post and the positions of the brigades and the battalions of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is that generally acceptable that they do not possess this kind of information?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I can answer your question very clearly from a military point of view. As regards the shelling of Sarajevo, it really wasn't necessary to know where the chief of the unit was. The most important thing for us was to know where the positions occupied by the men on the contact line was. From that point, we could determine exactly whether the shells fired on Sarajevo were falling on military positions, plus or minus a few metres, and we want to be very clear here for the Tribunal that the location of the headquarters was not at all necessary in order to know exactly where the military or civilian points were. The point was that there was fighting and there was firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that, according to you, the point was that there was firing and that there was combat. Could you confirm, and this is the information that the Defence has --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I do not think -- I think that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, I did not finish my question. I would like you to confirm the information that the Defence has is that the Muslims, throughout the war that lasted three and a half years, carried out 88 operations; they launched operations and attacks from Sarajevo. Could you confirm that this figure that the Defence has is acceptable to you, how many of these operations were launched, these combats and attacks from the -- by the Muslims, by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, Madam, first of all, I will finish my answer to your question about the lines and the headquarters. I repeat that we knew the contact lines and the positions of the troops. The exact delineations between the units had very little importance for us. As regards the fighting, and I am speaking here only about the period of my command, I could tell you that every day, almost every day, there was an exchange of fire on the contact line between the various parties. There were contacts which take place -- I repeat this -- took place almost every day. You are now mentioning the number of 88 or -- alleged operations by the Muslims that were launched from the Sarajevo zone. The figure which you are giving, well, I don't know whether it covers the whole war, only the period of my command. This figure, for me, as the commander of the United Nations troops, whether it is 88 or 40 or 68, it all comes down to the same thing: After a certain amount of time, the Muslim troops were in the position to organise themselves and to launch attacks from Sarajevo, attacks about which we have already spoken a great deal with Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we would like to consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, you spoke of the agreement for Mount Igman signed in 1993. You said that the Serbs handed over to the UN, to the UNPROFOR, a part of Igman that they held and Mount Bjelasnica. Now, according to you, was this an obligation of UNPROFOR for that part of Mount Igman to prevent active operation by Muslim troops from the safe zone of Sarajevo, that part of Mount Igman that was handed over to them by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that one cannot connect - cannot - the Mount Igman operations from those from Sarajevo. The agreement on Mount Igman was wished by Mr. Stoltenberg, and I repeat, it was carried out properly by the two parties. General Mladic accepted it for the first time, agreed to withdraw to Mount Igman, that is, to set up positions beyond the lines that were set up by the United Nations, and the Muslim troops deployed behind the line which had been set in the same way by the United Nations staff. And I repeat, it was more difficult for them than the Serbs. It was probably more difficult for them also. The operation on Mount Igman had, as its essential purpose, and I repeat this, to calm down the situation on the ground so that the major military operations could be finished in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the Stoltenberg-Owen negotiations with the different parties. In light of the area of Mount Igman, I don't think that it was possible to launch operations, military operations, on a large scale at the point that we were on Mount Igman. Because neither party had the available infantry troops in order to control such a wooded surface.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, if I tell you, if I put it to you that the Muslim army from Mount Igman that was under the control of UNPROFOR launched offensive operations in the direction of parts of Mount Igman that were under the control of Republika Srpska, do you have such information that these operations were carried out by the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in the first days of executing the Mount Igman agreement, General Delic had much more difficulty carrying out the orders than the Serb part of General Galic. And I think that in the first days of August, the Muslim troops were trying to take back control of two hills, but which were lower than 500 or 600 metres, and it is true that there was a constant effort on the part of the UN troops to have the Muslim troops withdraw. And I would even say that there was an exchange of fire between the United Nations troops and the Muslim troops. A French captain was very seriously wounded at that time and that caused a very, very strong reaction from General Cot to Mr. Izetbegovic. So in the beginning, the Muslim troops tried to infiltrate into certain areas, to take them back. But I think that, in general, the agreement was respected because in 1995, that was where the rapid reaction forces under the command of General Soubirou deployed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, if I put it to you that in this -- General, in this area, if I put it to you that UNPROFOR took control of the part of Mount Igman which was under the control of the BH army, the BH army carried out an attack and massacred a Serb battalion, four nurses were massacred at the time. In the course of your mandate, did you receive this information or any such information?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any information. And I would tell you that I am very surprised that General Mladic never spoke to me about that, if, in fact, that happened. And so I said to you a little while ago, I know that there were operations conducted mainly in the early August by the Muslim troops, but I repeat that General Mladic never spoke to me about that type of incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will now let my colleague take over the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, before that happens, I note that in her last question, Ms. Pilipovic has put a proposition to the witness. It would be appropriate, in my respectful submission, for her to indicate the date that that event was claimed to have occurred. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it of any importance after the witness said he has no knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is important in a sense that it seems to be part of the Defence case, putting propositions, and given the fact that the General was in his position for some six months, if she knows the date, then that should be put or indicated, for the benefit of the Chamber rather than the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think I did say during the mandate of the General when he was in Sarajevo, if he had received such an information. I believe that is how I phrased my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but do you have a date? Or, I mean, you are talking about a certain incident. If it is part of the case of the Defence, then it would be appropriate to put to the witness what, in the view of the Defence, happened and when it happened. Let me just see.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just say, if you said: "In the course of your mandate." The transcript reads: "In the course of your mandate, did you receive this information or any such information?" Well, receiving the information during the mandate is not necessarily the same as the incident having taken place during the mandate. So if you could be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, in the course of your mandate, were you informed of the incident when a battalion was massacred, battalion of the army of Republika Srpska in Mount Igman, when four nurses were massacred; or perhaps you may have received this information after the end of your mandate?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that does nothing to respond to the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that it is the case of the Defence that this happened during the mandate of the General?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has the information that this took place in September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could put that to the witness. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Are you aware of such an attack that happened --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such an incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...such an incident --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I repeat the answer that I gave a few minutes ago. I received no information from General Mladic about those events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not from anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From no one else. If you will excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a clear answer. You don't know anything about it. You have no information about it. So, therefore, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, good morning.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for being here and thank you for the clarity of your answers. I will cross-examine you in French, and I thank you in advance for being very careful as to the cursor which is moving in front of your eyes on the transcript, because everything we say will be interpreted in both languages and we have to be very careful about this. Thank you in advance. General, you said on several occasions, and I am going to quote in French, how can it happen that Sarajevo is not shelled. And then later on you said it was impossible to avoid certain civilian areas. And then at another point in time, you said that the age of the ammunition caused naturally mistakes in firing. And at another time you said, that is in December 1993, that the BH army was preparing its operations from the civilian area. Do you remember if that is what you said; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, and starting from these facts, when you say that it is impossible to avoid the shelling of Sarajevo, you want to say at the same time that the age of the ammunition was naturally causing mistakes in firing; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in some cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You also want to say the smallness of the area and the proximity of the combat areas and the so-called urban area would obviously give cause to such kind of shelling; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will not answer by saying "yes or no" because I think I've got to given an explanation. I think that when a contact line crosses a city or in which two parties are fighting because both parties believe that they can win the war, it is inevitable that if one uses mortar artillery, there will be shells that fall on areas that could be called civilian areas. That seems to be very clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, thank you for your answer. Therefore, you are saying that the shelling of Sarajevo was meaning -- that you gave your answer that it was unavoidable. Inasmuch as what you said --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that it became inevitable from the point that the Bosnian troops decided to conduct military operations from safe areas. Admittedly, it wasn't inevitable when the Bosnian troops were not carrying out any operations in Sarajevo. But from the time - and I believe I have already answered seven or eight times the same question - at the point the both parties decided to wage war against each other, it became inevitable that when there was an exchange of artillery fire, that there would be shells falling on areas where there were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, thank you for your answer. However, I don't think that you answered the question I am going to ask you about Sarajevo. You said that the BH army was preparing their military operations from some kind of rear base which was located in civilian areas. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a military point of view, I don't know what you mean by "rear base" in Sarajevo, when you look at the limits of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We will come to that. We will come to that, General. But let us just say that was behind the lines.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you are saying something which is very obvious in terms of military matters. When an attack is being prepared, of course it is being prepared behind the contact line that one crosses in order to conquer a territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, General, when you say this is evident for you, it is not evident for everyone else, this obviousness to prepare an operation in the background behind the lines, and that is certainly evident that whatever is happening in this zone at the back, then becomes -- that area then becomes a legitimate area for the firing?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are continuing a discussion -- is this a military discussion that we are continuing, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A question has been put to you and it seems that a military aspect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will answer. It is very technical in military terms but I am going to answer as a professional. From the point when two parties have decided to wage war and one party notes that an operation is being prepared, if one has identified the exact spot where the preparations are taking place, from a strictly military point of view, you can attack those making the preparations. So it becomes a normal target. It is always that way that things happen in our military instructions of Western democracies. I cannot give any other answer. And I emphasise this, that when two parties have decided to fight, the military objectives become normal ones for both parties who are fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, General, and obviously we are not as expert as you are. That is the reason we are asking these questions. When two sides are waging war, are fighting, is it true that throughout your stay in Sarajevo that two sides were -- considered themselves in the state of war?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is very clear. When I arrived in July, the Serbs were shelling Sarajevo, whereas the Muslim troops were not preparing any operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The question was not to find out whether people were shelling each other or not, but whether the two sides, General, were considering themselves during the time of your stay as being in a state of armed conflict or in a state of war?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the period of my command, since there was no peace agreement, the three parties to the conflict considered themselves as being in a state of war, one in respect of the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, General. Now, I would like you to answer briefly to the following questions, and I am talking about a principal, these questions have -- cover a general aspect rather than the practical aspect in the situation of Sarajevo, but a general aspect. . Now, General, is it true - and if you can answer by "yes" or "no," I would be very grateful - it is true that a command post is a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: A command post, when it is identified, is a legitimate target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. General, is it true that a command post is a legitimate military target, whether it is on the level of a brigade, the level of a battalion or on the level of a company?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever the command post, I have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I am repeating that we are not answers -- we are not experts, but your answers are extremely important to us. General, the installations of communications and telecommunications, the facilities of such type, were also -- can also be considered as being military targets?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were identified as command posts, because when you say communications and telecommunications that is connected to command posts, I answer, yes. If they are communications facilities where civilian telecommunications, I would say, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, if installations or telecommunications, civilian telecommunications, are used for military purposes, do they then become technically, from a military aspect, do they then become legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are sure that those facilities are being used for military communications, then I would say, yes, as a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarity of your answer, General. I appreciate that. Now, a military vehicle or military vehicles, are they legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for the obviousness of your answer. Now civilian vehicles, General, that are used exclusively for military purposes, do they become legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would tend to say, yes, but I would say in order to be sure that they are being used for military purposes, that is not always so clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I completely agree with you. But my answer was about the type of the vehicle. So your answer is "yes" in relation to the vehicles, if I understand correctly, General?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered that if one can determine that the civilian vehicles are being used in military operations or being used by military people, then they become a military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. General, were you or your services informed of the fact that - and I have to tell you that we have multiple testimonies in this respect - that certain vehicles which were originally of civilian character, for instance, Volkswagen Golf vehicles, were used to transport mortars from which then attacks were launched. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that all the possible and imaginable vehicles were being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The last half dozen words of that question do not reflect the evidence. "Were used to transport mortars," and then these following words are the important ones: "from which then attacks were launched." I also make the fundamental objection to, in this type of context, my learned colleague informing the witness of what he thinks other witnesses have said. It bears no relevance with this type of question. More fundamentally, I am not aware of evidence, certainly from multiple witnesses, that mortars were launched from Golf cars. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you rephrase your question and perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, again, I would suggest that the French channel should be listened to. That would be a lot clearer for everyone. And I think that the General understood my question. It is technically not possible to fire from a Golf; that can be very dangerous. Attacks were carried out with mortars. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...blame the other party for not listening to the right channel. I am changing from channel again and again. The question was whether you had any information about civilian vehicles, Volkswagen Golfs, used to transport mortars and then mortars being fired in connection with this transportation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very specifically, I would say, no, to the question. In general terms, this was one of my fears, that all the vehicles, and I say all vehicles, all possible and imaginable vehicles were being used by all the parties. And I would add, Mr. President, because I think that is important, that United Nations vehicles were car-jacked and that caused me a great deal of concern. I believe that I have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So no specific knowledge of mortars being transported in civilian vehicles, at least vehicles with a civilian appearance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did you or your intelligence services, did you know of the existence of small lorries or small trucks, and we have testimony to this effect, from which it was possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it is of no use in this context to tell the witness what the evidence was already. It may sometimes have some use, but not here. So would you please refrain from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise, Mr. President. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, do you or your intelligence or information services, did you know about lorries, small lorries from which it was possible or -- rather, it was possible to fire mortars that were mounted on them; they became mobile mortars?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know, General -- do you know of the fact that General Morillon had to protest the Presidency, that is the Presidency of Sarajevo, in relation to the shots that were fired from the hospital compound of the -- the compound of the Kosevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I took over General Morillon's command, he didn't speak to me about that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just answered that he did not speak to me about that problem. And if General Morillon did not speak to me about it, then I attributed no importance to all kinds of rumours I heard coming from everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, General I understand, but my question was the following, if you can answer precisely. That is why I am rephrasing the question. I am asking the question again. The General didn't speak to you, but when you left, did you know about this?
