utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no specific knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, I would like us to go to another line of questioning, but in order to respect the time, because I can see that the president is looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, how much time have we got left, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you would have another -- a bit less than an hour. Approximately 50, 55 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, I would like you to answer this question: Did you know whether in Sarajevo some schools were used by the army, either for tactical purposes or in order to use them instead of barracks which were not existent?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You say "no"?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You don't know it. Very well. Colonel -- I apologise -- General, I would like us to go back to another question now. You said that when some shelling took place on the areas that you considered as being civilian areas, you would intervene personally with the military authorities in question. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I think I have already answered that question several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. But you didn't answer this one: What was the effect, the result, of your intervention? Was there a marked decrease in the shelling?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered that question, also. We often noted that there was a drop, which I wouldn't say was lasting, but there was a drop in the amount of firing after our interventions. That happened rather frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is that the rule?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was rather the rule, until November.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, I would like us to go back to some other questions. Do you know what is a C4? The C4.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that doesn't mean anything to me, C4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, I will surprise you, General, that is an explosive which is used to blow buildings up.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not an explosives export.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Neither am I, but I will not ask that question. General, do you know if in Sarajevo there was considerable black market specifically in relation to products that were -- or produce that was imported or brought in by humanitarian aids?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I answered a question of Mr. Ierace on that subject. I was well aware that there was a black market in Sarajevo that was the subject of an investigation. And I remember the visit of an Austrian General, General Grandel, who came to investigate the problem of the black market. He really annoyed us quite a bit -- or that "it" annoyed us. Yes, it is true that there was a problem of black market in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, is it true, was it possible to find produce that was brought in by the humanitarian aid which was then being resold in certain markets, for instance, in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not refer to Tuzla. I would simply say that when humanitarian aid was distributed, certain inhabits of Sarajevo preferred to be hungry so that they could read or smoke a cigarette, et cetera. So we were very aware that humanitarian rations were sold among the population, whether resold on the Tuzla market, that I don't know. But it is so that we were very aware that when we gave out humanitarian assistance to someone, it was assistance that he could do with what he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Now, did you know, General, whether this black market was organised on another level, on a more organised criminal level?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no evidence, no proof about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. You say you have no proof, but do you at least have a feeling about this?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a city under siege like Sarajevo, I can well imagine that some people got rich on the black market, and I explained that at great length in my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am going to ask you to give me the references. I will certainly have a look at it. I don't know whether the Chamber will read it. So could I consider your answer as being yes?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a completely personal opinion. It seems to me that the black market was organised beyond the level of individual level of inhabitants of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, General. I would like to go back to the shelling. You said earlier, asked by the Prosecution, that, "As a general rule, the Serbs, since we are talking about the Serb army, was shelling most the military targets. They were more targeting military targets than civilian targets. In fact, I intervened." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If you confirm if this is the case, that the material destruction, the most important material destruction that took place that was as a result of the shelling took place in Sarajevo, occurred in Sarajevo in the areas which were areas in the vicinity of the confrontation lines or in the vicinity of the combat areas? I am talking about Otes, for instance, or again in areas that were near strategic incontestable military targets, strategic targets. I am talking about near the Dobrinja market. Could you perhaps confirm this as principle?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I have answered that question. I believe that I said it was very difficult to answer by saying, "yes" or "no." Perhaps I could add an additional comment --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, I have to interrupt. I don't think that this question was asked. My question was the following: Is it true, yes or no, that material damages in buildings and urban structures were the most important in the areas, more considerable in the areas near combat areas, near combat areas or near strategic targets?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't answer by "yes" or "no," and for the following reason: During the periods of my command, perhaps I could answer "yes." But when I arrived in Sarajevo, what surprised me the most was to see the amount of significant destruction throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But I was talking about the most significant damage. Can I consider, General, that in relation to the phrasing of my question, the most significant damage, would you agree with me then?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by, "the most significant damage." When I went through Sarajevo along what was called "sniping alley," almost all the buildings or civilian apartments were burned or destroyed or had been shelled. That was what I noted when I arrived in Sarajevo. And I repeat that throughout my stay in Sarajevo, thanks to the action that we conducted, I had the impression - and this is a completely personal impression but for me it is a certainty - that essentially from October to December, essentially, military objectives were shelled more than civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarity of your question [sic], General. General, I would like us to go on to some technical questions. Did you personally know, and I know that without a map it is very difficult, but did you know yourself, did you know the depth of the lines of the separation in Sarajevo, demarcation lines of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like in all cities, the contact lines, I recall -- sorry, went from several metres, from several dozen metres, because from that point on you can't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, General. Now, I would like us to have a look at the question of ceasefires. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. We know, and you told us, that ceasefires were -- either didn't hold or were never signed. Do you know if on the side of the Presidency, there was in some way a political will not to accept ceasefires -- ceasefire in Sarajevo, and only for political reasons. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer here by mentioning what I wrote in my book about that. And this is the general idea that I had of the situation in Sarajevo. Sarajevo could not be a calm city because for the Bosnian Presidency, if nothing happened any more in Sarajevo, that would mean that people would never -- would not continue to speak about Bosnia-Herzegovina in the outside world. And for the Serbs, Sarajevo could not remain calm either because Sarajevo was a way of putting constant pressure in order to make the Muslims sign a peace agreement. Therefore, I was well aware of that fact and, moreover, the situation could not remain calm for a long time in Sarajevo because of that. In fact, both parties were uninterested in having a calm situation in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, General. I would like, because of the rules of the cross-examination, I would like to ask you to answer as briefly as possible to my questions. I am going to come back to the Muslim side in the conflict. Should I interpret your answer as saying that you are answering "yes" in a sense that the Muslim side did not wish to have a ceasefire for political reasons?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that proposal. Because now I am going to say how I felt -- our experience of the negotiations that were going on. The Muslim side always hoped that NATO would become involved in a decisive way in respect of a peace agreement. This was the -- or rather one of the main objects -- objectives of Izetbegovic, that is, to make NATO intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, I am going to have to interrupt you, because that was my line of questioning. So I will continue in this direction so that things become clearer. Are you saying that the attitude of the Presidency in Sarajevo at a given time, at the time that you have known during your stay, consisted of -- consisted in refusing immediate peace through ceasefires or other agreements, hoping to be able to obtain, in one way or another, an intervention, a NATO intervention that you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat what I think I have already said. Mr. Izetbegovic accepted, or would have anticipated a peace agreement -- would have accepted the Stoltenberg-Owen peace agreement so long that NATO would make him absolutely sure that the peace agreement would be respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. General, were you informed of the fact that when some ceasefires were obtained, that this was either de facto or de lege, the parties, the sides in the conflict, but in fact it was the Muslim side which would then provoke, through firing, through shooting, in the hope of destroying the ceasefire, either legal or factual?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I would say to you that the three parties to the conflict all ignored the ceasefire. I would not like to give a better role to one than to another of those parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But isn't it, however, true that in relation to the question, in respect to the question that I asked you, General, the provocations came in with this particular purpose?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered that the three parties, according to their own interests, would --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But you did not answer sufficiently clearly, at least for me. Is it true, yes or no, General, that the Muslim side were provoking in the military sense, in order to undermine the ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did the same thing as all the other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for your answer. General, do you know or were you informed at the time of your stay in Sarajevo of a situation, a rather specific situation, where the Muslim side tried, and sometimes in a very dramatic way, to draw the attention on itself for political purposes, for the purpose of sensitising the press presenting the situation as being theirs? Did you know about that or were you informed about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the last word of that question, I did not hear. I think the transcript is catching up now. Thank you. I have no further comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you, sir, what do you mean "sometimes"? Or what do you mean when you say "a dramatic situation"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will answer later but this is my next question but, General, can you answer in principle and I will continue in more details if you want

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to answer but once you've explained what you mean by -- when you say "very dramatic."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, General. What I was trying to say is that we believe that, on some occasions, Muslim forces either exploited the situation of human misery or in the media or were directly provoking the situations causing the situation of human misery in order to draw attention on themselves. The question is: Were you personally informed of this or your intelligence services or other services, did they know about this?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could answer by a sentence which is on the back of the McKenzie's book, the Canadian General who was the first commander in Sarajevo, and he said that "If I could convince both parties, and I say both parties, that they should not fight -- should not fire on one zone population in order to please CNN, that would be progress." I have no proof, therefore, that one party fired on its own people in order to provoke a media explosion. I would say that in Sarajevo it was very tempting for the Muslims, of course, to use as much as they could all the media, the international media, present in Sarajevo, in order to defend their own cause. They did so. And since you are the Defence counsel, I would also say what I said, and I think that I said it yesterday in answer to a question of Mr. Ierace, the Serb side did not realise that by shelling Sarajevo the way it was doing, it was losing all its credit with the international community. I believe that I can say to you that it was extremely difficult for the UNPROFOR forces, commanders, to remain objective and measured in the light of this extraordinary media pressure, and that one can be understood in respect of the parties, that this media coverage was being exploited for their own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we are being informed that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would this be a suitable time for the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, I would like us to continue along the line that we followed before the break. You said, quoting a sentence on the last page or on the back page of the book written by a colleague, General McKenzie. Personally speaking, do you personally agree with this sentiment that was expressed?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to answer that question. My personal impression has absolutely nothing to do with what we are talking about. I am simply going to speak about facts that I noted myself. If I didn't do it, I take no position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. General, I am going to come back to the black market question. Is it true, and this is a fact, that the fuel which was lacking, there was a shortage of fuel in Sarajevo, the actual market of fuel was controlled by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the fuel market was in the hands of the Muslim army, but in light of the situation in Sarajevo, from a strictly professional point of view, I would say that it was normal that the Muslims would control the use of gasoline that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I understand that you have written a book. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can I assume that you were particularly well-documented as to what went on in Sarajevo in order to be able to write this book. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base myself on all the documentation that I had, letters, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you made this effort, I believe, after your stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did it after my stay in Sarajevo and I would even say after I was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. General, thank you. Therefore you have a distance and you were able to base yourself on the perhaps more numerous pieces of information than you had at the time when -- during your stay in Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I based myself only on what I had personally experienced in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. General, you were responsibility for Sarajevo in Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the commander of the UN forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was responsible for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of course including Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. So the answer is "yes." So in this capacity, you must know a large number of things. So in order to gain time, I am going to now give you a list of names and I would like you to tell me, very briefly, by a yes or no if you know to what this corresponds and where this is. I am going now: Sultan Fatih?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Pavle Goranin?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Petar Dakic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Could I stop for a moment here? I gave a long explanation yesterday to the Tribunal that I would have discussions with Mr. Izetbegovic, with General Delic. I know both of their deputies, the Serb, the Croat, and I don't know all those names. I have no memory of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. This is not people, these are locations. Kobra?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Kulin Ban --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Having said, "This is not people, these are locations," the next question or name or word that my friend added was Kobra. I gather that Kobra does not in fact refer to a location and perhaps that illustrates to -- perhaps that illustrates the difficulty in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. simply running words with no description past a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the other hand, Mr. Ierace, if we ask Mr. Piletta-Zanin to tell us a lot about it, he always pronounces it very quickly. So perhaps if he could pronounce it more quietly and then it is a very quick way to find out whether it does ring a bell at all with the witness. All explanations, to finally come to the answer that the witness doesn't know anything about it, is not very efficient as well. So, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed but keep in mind that at a high speed mentioning 10 or 15 or 20 names, well, might cause a lot of confusion and misunderstanding. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Kobra?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't mean anything to me. And I would like to add a comment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Briquemont, the Defence counsel is trying to find out whether certain names, these might be perhaps names of places or institutions or whether they are familiar to you. Because if they are not familiar, it might be of no use at all to ask any further questions. So he goes through the list of his names. If they do not ring a bell, please tell us that. Just by saying "no" would be enough. And if they do ring a bell, perhaps there are some additional questions. Yes. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you in advance. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, the question -- the answer is "no" to Kobra. Kulin Ban?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Does the factory Zrak mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Does Zetra mean anything to you? Zetra which is one of the facilities, one of the halls, which was made for the Olympic Games. Was that used as a warehouse by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zetra?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Zetra.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was occupied during my command period by a battalion of the FrenchBat company. So Zetra was occupied by the UN troops during my command at the time. At the end of July of 1993, we had a serious incident there. And yesterday, I said that Mr. Karadzic even apologised to the UN forces for that incident which had caused the loss of several UN vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Does the name Kazani mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I would now like to come back to the question of snipers. You said in your earlier declaration followed by a question asked by the Prosecution that the sniping activity, BH snipers was not in any way less than the Serb snipers. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say that the activity was in no way less intense, do you mean quantitatively or in terms of quality?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would answer in terms of quantity. And qualitatively, I think I answered at length that question that was asked by Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So what you saying is that there is no difference, there was no difference, in terms of quality, that is the way that the snipers were used on either side?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In respect of the use of snipers, I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object. As translated into the English language, the question goes to the quality of sniping, which in my respectful submission does not make sense. If my friend means by that that he is enquiring as to whether snipers were used equally against military personnel and civilians, then he should say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, "quality" could mean a lot of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. But I believe that the answer that the General was going to give was also very clear. Perhaps he can repeat it because I think that he understood the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, a clear answer to an unclear question is not what we are seeking. But if you -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Was it used in the same way on both sides?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was used for the same purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interfere. The purposes could be different purposes. If you say in the same purposes, I still do not know what the purpose was. Was the purpose to shoot at military or to shoot at civilians? You said it was the same on both sides. Could you explain to us what the purpose was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe very sincerely, Mr. President, that the objectives were basically civilians in order to put pressure on the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, in your capacity as a professional, could you tell us what a sniper is, as far as you know, according to your experience?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: A sniper is what one calls an elite firer, that is someone who has -- who shoots a weapon over a great distance, and that weapon is used to hit individual targets from a long distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, you spoke in your testimony yesterday about uncontrolled elements. That was page 79, line 6. When you were speaking of uncontrolled elements, General, do you also mean to say what I would tend to call "quasi-snipers," that is, individuals who were not members of an army but who were -- in some way were playing at judges?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I answered that question yesterday. The snipers were a constant and serious concern for us. I had the personal opinion or, rather, impression there were armed people - allow me to say it - they were playing at being snipers. It was something very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say that they were people who were armed who were playing as snipers, and I apologise, General, for coming back to that, but what is clear to you after many months on the ground is not obviously clear for Defence counsel or anyone else. When you are speaking of people, people who were armed, you are talking about people who were not members of an army, that is, in other words, these were individuals, these were civilians then?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a personal impression. But I had the impression that they were people who were armed, who had weapons, and who were not members of any organised army. That is a personal impression, I repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for your impression. But since you were on the ground and in the field, we need your impressions in order for the truth to come out. You say that these people were armed. Did they have access or could they also have automatic weapons? We know, for instance, AK-47 or the Kalashnikov was very wide-spread in the countries of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But Kalashnikov has nothing to do with a marksman's weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Indeed. But what you are saying is that the people who were individuals also had elite weapons?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps not so sophisticated weapons as we might have in the United Nations -- among the United Nations troops. But Kalashnikovs does not allow precise firing beyond 150 or 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So, General, I conclude from your answer is that these armed persons that you do not believe were part of a military structure had weapons of -- high-precision weapons?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily high-precision, but I can tell you that there are weapons that make it possible to fire from 400 to 500 metres with relatively great accuracy. They can be used as second-category snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, could you please be a little bit specific on the type of the weapon? Could you give us one or two examples of this type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I take the case that I am the best familiar with, the weapons of my country, we have ordinary rifles that do fire, if used by good people, up to distances of 400 to 500 metres. The Kalashnikov is an automatic weapon which does not allow a very precise fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, when you -- I think we have a problem of an echo. I don't know whether this is just in my headphones, but I will continue. General, whether you are talking about sniping weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am keeping very strict to the time. You have eight minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, when you are speaking about weapons, marksman weapons, sniper weapons, high-precision weapons, are you then speaking of the automatic firing?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. So you are talk about automatic bursts. They are not linked to the sniper weapons?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, General. Now I would like us to have a look at some other questions that are in relation to civilian areas. What do you mean in general by "civilian area"?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: A civilian area is a zone which people live and where there is no possible military objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, General. Therefore, a residential area where there would be a command post or a strategic facility that had military importance, then that is no longer a civilian area. Is that correct, as far as you are concerned?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are a speaking about one building, I would say that the building, or I would say that the floor where a command post was identified becomes a military objective, but certainly not the area around that building. So I make a very clear distinction between a building, a location, and I would even say a floor, when I think about Sarajevo, that could become a military target, but certainly not the area around that dwelling or that floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. So you rule out all mistakes of firing?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: A firing error, well, I would say that is always possible. But if you take a 20-floor building, you might make a mistake as to the floor, but not fire at the building next door.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, General. Now, I am going to come back to one of the consequences of the conventions, the convention that you know extremely well. Isn't it true that when we are in such a situation, combat in an urban area, there is an obligation between the warring parties to look to create neutral zones on the level of civilian populations, that is, if need be, to remove the populations away from the front line?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, General, that is theory perhaps but, please, could you answer as a witness, quasi-expert witness? Could you answer my question, please, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. even if it is theoretical?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't try to do that in Sarajevo. It was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, General, my question is the following: Isn't it true that, normally speaking, that the text makes this point very clear?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the text makes it clear, then I would say, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Do you know, General, if the Muslim side did exactly this in Sarajevo, if they carried out this movement of their own population in the areas of combat or near the areas of the separation, in the areas of separation, demarcation lines?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: As much as I can remember, I would say that the civilians themselves did so. I don't think that the Sarajevo government took that problem over but in fact -- in light of the fact that the city was very small, moving the population from one point to another in the city didn't mean very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Here what you mean, you said earlier that it was impossible. So what you are saying is that the city was far too small in order to do -- to carry this out?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not that the city was too small, but in light of the contact light around the city, there was no sense in moving a significant number of people from one area to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: For the reason that they would have been near another combat line?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just one issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You were asked questions whether the fuel in Sarajevo was controlled by the army and also whether there was a shortage of fuel in Sarajevo. Were there -- what were the sources of fuel, and I mean by that all of the sources of fuel, during your time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose -- I say "I suppose" because I have no specific information about that. I suppose that the available fuel in Sarajevo was the fuel stocked in Sarajevo at the beginning of the war. But I wondered also about the problem of the black market, black market in fuel, and I would say then, when we would do something in Sarajevo, for instance, when we tried to open some of the roads or sometimes to allow the Oslobodjenje newspaper to operate, the UN troops would provide the necessary fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say you wondered also about the problem of the black market, did you have any information as to whether any of the UN forces were operating on the black market in terms of supplying fuel on the black market?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had one specific case in a UN battalion that was in Sarajevo and which triggered an investigation, or I had an investigation started into that, on that occasion. We had the feeling that some soldiers were selling a few litres of fuel on the black market. I think that a litre of fuel was selling for about 35 marks, and so there was a lot of temptation sometimes for some of the soldiers who came from countries that weren't very rich to do what I would say become small black marketeers without any mafia organisation behind that. But it discredited the UN troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How did the hotels and other commercial establishments in Sarajevo obtain fuel?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, you are asking a good question there. I have no specific answer to give you because I really believe that there was a black market in petrol for which -- well, when there was an investigation, it was independent, it was not under my control. And therefore one would perhaps have to try to find the conclusions of the investigations that were conducted during my command period. They must exist at the staff, of the UNPROFOR staff in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, one other issue, Mr. President. You were also asked questions in cross-examination about what was described as quasi-snipers, and you were asked as to whether they were part of any army. What was your view, if you had one, as to whether the command of the Serb forces could have stopped those individuals from sniping against civilians, if they had so wished?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am going to give you a very clear answer. If the Serb authorities and the Muslim authorities - and I am first thinking about the political authorities of both sides - had they wanted to impose -- put an end to all of the snipers, whether quasi-snipers or others, they could have. And I think that I said yesterday, when I answered one of your questions, that no political official, whatever he was, ever disavowed publicly the sniper activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask for a clarification, please. You said earlier, as I understood - I understood that you said - that when you arrived in July, the city of Sarajevo was being shelled intensely and that, in your opinion, this was not a response to a provocation or even a response to preparations. Therefore, you mean that the shelling -- well, how would you characterise it militarily? Could one think that it was aiming at the civilians or that there were military objectives which could have been the target of that shelling?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I arrived in Sarajevo, that corresponded -- it corresponded the most to shelling which had nothing to do with military objectives. And I indicated a few minutes ago that I was surprised to see the extent of the destruction in the city, throughout the city, when I arrived in Sarajevo, which meant that before I arrived, the city of Sarajevo had been hit everywhere or almost everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you as well. You have told us extensively on what happened in the beginning of December 1993. You have told us to be surprised to receive complaints from the BiH side about shelling, since they prepared or launched an attack themselves. Was the type of shelling the BiH was complaining about, was that shelling with a clear military purpose or was that the type of shelling you just described in response to the question of Judge El Mahdi, that means shelling without a clear military purpose?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would say that as opposed to the beginning of July, the shelling in December was shelling between two armies which were trying to destroy one -- trying to destroy military targets, essentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is clear to me. You have told us about people playing snipers, as you expressed it. Could you give us any idea of what percentage of snipers of each side would be quasi-snipers of those playing snipers, and have you any knowledge of snipers within the regular forces?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me answer on three points. When I say that they were playing at snipers or quasi-snipers, I would like to give you two examples that I experienced myself. It happened that when my vehicle was going along sniper alley, there was -- a metre in front or behind my vehicle, there was shelling. At another time, it was more important, when I arrived at the airport, there was a sniper that fired at the vehicle, trying to hit the motor. So I don't think they were trying to hit someone in the vehicle. I think they were very specific and clear type sniping. That is what I call quasi-sniping or playing at snipers. I think that terrorised the population. I was given other examples. That is the first point. The second point: Yesterday I said, Mr. President, that the French Battalion had identified several sniper positions. I believe that those positions were held by snipers under Muslim and under Serb control. To say -- to tell you what the percentage of real snipers or quasi-snipers was, that I cannot do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I better understand that quasi-snipers of those playing snipers were not necessarily outside the regular forces. It was more the way they are using their weapons than their place in the military structure?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say, Mr. President, in order to answer more clearly, that among these snipers that I would characterise as military, there were also those playing at snipers. Is my answer clearer now, more precise? I would tell you that in the afternoon, that is when it was the most difficult period because, in the afternoon, most of the people who were playing at snipers already had drunk quite a bit of alcohol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Briquemont, that concludes your testimony -- just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but you asked two or three questions that gave answers, lengthy answers, by the General and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...not new subjects touched upon. I mean, the subjects have been dealt with both in examination-in-chief and in cross-examination, and I think that is the criteria we use. If there is a new issue touched upon by the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just one point. General Briquemont was a lot more specific now in terms of aspects of destruction in the city of Sarajevo, not just on the borders, so to speak, of Sarajevo. It was on this point that we would like to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...has been dealt with during the cross-examination and I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, we won't ask this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is just one question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we allow you to do it but -- and that is also because of the situation of time at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, General, you spoke of the significant destruction in Sarajevo, that is in July of 1993, when you arrived. So in relation to what you said, how can you rule out categorically, General, the possibility that in relation to such-and-such and some other destruction that you saw at the moment when the firing occurred, the shots occurred, or when mobile targets were there or maybe some other legitimate military targets like vehicles that were transporting troops, or troops in movement? Could you rule out that they were there at the time?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I remember everything that I saw in Sarajevo along the new city or all the -- all the buildings - I have quite a number of photographs at home - there were buildings of 10 to 15 storeys where everything was destroyed. I can say that, as a military man, those Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. buildings were a target of systematic firing before I arrived. Because when you speak to me about mobile vehicles who might have been using mortars, you know, to fire a mortar from the 7th floor of a building is almost impossible. So, categorically, I would say that when we see the scope of the destruction on all of the buildings where people lived, all along Sniper Alley, that meant that those buildings were the systematic target of firing before I came.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, my question was the following: You saw destruction, as you said, not only in the sniper alley, which we discussed at great length, but in the entire city. Could you, yes or no, rule out that at the time the shooting occurred, and you did not witness it, there were no mobile military targets in that location?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in my respectful submission, the answer quite clearly did answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. General Briquemont, did I understand your answer well that although one might not exclude for certain that the damage might have been damage caused by the presence -- at the time the damage was done by the presence of any military object, either mobile or only temporarily located in that specific place, that the extent of the damage as a whole could hardly be explained by the presence of such military targets at so many places and -- is that what your answer tells us?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMONT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question has been answered, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. [Interpretation] Since there are no further questions, I hesitate to say this, but that completes your testimony before this Chamber. General, I thank you for having come to The Hague and for having answered all the questions asked by the parties and the Chamber. And I will now ask the usher to escort you outside the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, to save time, I seek only to tender one document, which is P3717. There are also two matters I would seek to raise at some stage in the next 10 minutes. One of those matters is a response to the request that you made yesterday afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please guide us through the limited number of documents, only one being tendered at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Prosecutor's Exhibit 3717 is a graph entitled State Hospital Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and do we have any -- we have, I think, one document but I do not -- was it just to be read? You have given us page 3 of a Security Council resolution but it bears no number. It is, of course, a perfectly-known source of law or politics - I don't know - but you do not tender that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do apologise. I do seek to tender the resolution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You seek to tender the resolution as a whole or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Mr. President. We believe that it is authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...one of the things the parties could easily compromise on. Thank you. So, then additionally Exhibit P3715, Security Council Resolution 836, is tendered by the Prosecution. And since there are no objections, both the documents are admitted and are exhibits now. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in response to the inquiry that you made yesterday afternoon, I do not have any objection to the Defence retaining a copy of the material which was sent to them from the authorities in Republika Srpska, but I would not want that to be seen in any way as a precedent. But in this particular case, I have no difficulty with that. Secondly, during the examination-in-chief of this witness, I have become concerned as to the frequency of interruptions which come about as a result of complaints about the quality of translation. Those interjections have come from Mr. Piletta-Zanin and one notes that the pace of the interjections, the interruptions is increasing. In relation to the examination-in-chief of General Briquemont, there were 12, and I have counted them, 12 interruptions, because of concern by Mr. Piletta-Zanin about the quality of the translation, overwhelmingly the French translation. Of those 12, 5 related to the translation of the witness who spoke in French into English. During the testimony -- during the questioning of senior counsel for the Defence, Ms. Mara Pilipovic, there were no interruptions from Mr. Piletta-Zanin expressing concerns about the quality of the translation. And of course, when he was asking questions, there was none. But the appropriate comparison is with the questioning by Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. President, apart from the loss of time, it directly impacts on the flow of the witness's evidence. The interjection is usually made at the end of a question asked by me, so that following the completion of the interjection issue, the question then has to be re-asked, or the witness reread the question. Mr. President, I don't seek to delve into the issue of the appropriateness of the interjections but simply to point out that that is the inevitable consequences of them and they have now reached again, as they did before the occasion that I rose to my feet and raise this issue two weeks ago, they have now reached in frequency [Realtime transcript read in error "frequently"] a point where they are significantly impacting on the flow of evidence. I would be very grateful if the Trial Chamber could consider some other mechanism to deal with these matters. Given that, it apparently does not concern the Defence when they are asking questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will be very brief. Very brief. It is not true and I believe it is libelous. I intervene when Ms. Pilipovic was speaking, I was asking for rectification, and you can check it in the transcript if you are careful. I did it. Second thing: 89, line 2, "frequency" instead of "frequently." Third thing, Mr. Ierace himself trapped himself yesterday on a point that I had asked the English booth to check what they said. I did not say they were mounted on a vehicle, but they were transporting a vehicle. Now, if I am intervening, it is because it is necessary and I am keeping this to a minimum. What I did today, Mr. President, there were certain wrong meanings that were flagrant of what the witness was saying, that they were saying more military shelling, rather than civilian, and the English transcript was saying the contrary. Now if the Prosecution doesn't check, as we are doing, the English transcript, although it is a lot easier for them because there are more of them, then I will do it for them. But then I should not be criticised in doing what I have to do and I am in fact lifting the burden of the Prosecution for doing it and I am doing it at the minimum when I have to do it and the way I have to do it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will not be able, I am afraid, to solve this problem forever. But first of all, I would like to mention that quite -- at quite a number of occasions, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, while questioning the witness, was at the same time asking for correction of the translation into English of his own question. So the Chamber would not agree that he is just asking for corrections if the Prosecution is examining the witness. On the other hand, very often the correction does not immediately affect the witness. If a question is put to the witness in English, and when the witness speaks French, the Defence has a better reason to interfere, because it might be confusing for the witness. If, on the other hand, the witness is speaking the same language as the party that examines the witness, any requests in respect of correcting the translation could wait until after the question has been answered. The Chamber feels on the one hand that it is important not to disturb the flow of information given by the witness. On the other hand, if a translation which needs specific attention might affect the answer of the witness, then it should be done. And if, Mr. Ierace, if you tell us that it is mainly done at the end of your question just before the witness starts replying, then this might be caused also by the fact that the translation always is a bit behind. So if there is a problem halfway through your question, it might be only at the end of your question that the translation gives a clue that it needs specific attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I suggest another course that could perhaps have become the problem and that is where the issue does not affect the understanding by the witness of the question asked, that those issues be dealt with at the end of the testimony of the witness. In other words, we keep a record and then at least at the end of that day, we reserve 5 or 10 minutes to do the transcript correction so as not to impede the flow of evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, I am not a judge of my own comprehension of the witness a priori or a posteriori, I'm only worried about what he's hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the translation problem is just for the transcript, this does not affect the answer of the witness because he not even has heard the translation. Of course, with General Briquemont --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Depends on which language. It depends on the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider the matter whether we should -- if you want to make an observation as to saving all the comments as to the end of the day --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I must make a point is that technically when I wanted to use as many yellow pads as possible, the answer that was given to me by the court reporters was that the truth is what appears on the screen, not what we would like to bring in the modifications after the session is adjourned. This is what I try to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...question of Mr. Ierace. Mr. Ierace's suggestion is that we do it at the end of the hearing, not after the hearing has been closed. So it can be part of the transcript. We stop 5 minutes early to say line so and so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, I do understand that there is also a general procedure which allows any of the parties to submit comments on the transcript within 10 days to the Registry. I was not too well aware of that. But looking at the clock, we have to finish for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I see that that is also on the letter, first, the draft transcript will be distributed to the parties and then it continues, comments to be submitted by -- and then it gives another date. We will consider the matter, keeping in mind both the aspects, good translation and at the same time, an uninterrupted flow of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
